qs.q: A 72-year-old institutionalized man with Parkinson disease presents with rapid, massive abdominal distension, absolute constipation, and acute colicky lower abdominal pain. His abdomen is tense, tympanitic, and drum-like with an empty rectum on digital examination. There is no rebound tenderness or guarding. What is the most common underlying predisposing factor for this condition in African hospi
o: Prior abdominal surgery and peritoneal adhesions
Malignant stricture of the descending colon
A high-fibre diet with a long redundant sigmoid
Congenital aganglionic megacolon of the rectum
qs.e: Sigmoid volvulus is commonly predisposed to by a high-fibre diet leading to a bulky stool load and a long redundant sigmoid colon with a narrow-based mesentery. In African hospitals, it accounts for over 50% of intestinal obstructions, unlike Western nations where cancer is more frequent.
qs.s: Sigmoid and Caecal Volvulus: Diagnosis and Management: MCQs

qs.q: What is the core lesion in Parkinson's disease?
o: Intracellular accumulation of tau tangles in neurons
Spongiform change in the gray matter
Loss of dopaminergic neurons from the substantia nigra
Accumulation of Aβ plaques in the cerebral cortex
qs.e: The core lesion in Parkinson's disease is the loss of dopaminergic neurons from the substantia nigra, leading to reduced striatal dopamine. Aβ plaques and tau tangles are hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease, and spongiform change is characteristic of prion diseases.
qs.s: Neurodegenerative Prion Diseases: CJD, Pathology & Rapid Dementia: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following is a characteristic clinical feature of Parkinson's disease?
qs.e: Masked facies, along with tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia, are characteristic clinical features of Parkinson's disease. Startle myoclonus and rapidly progressive dementia are features of CJD, and extracellular PrP deposits are seen in prion diseases.
qs.s: Neurodegenerative Prion Diseases: CJD, Pathology & Rapid Dementia: MCQs

qs.q: How is the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease typically confirmed symptomatically?
o: Presence of neurofibrillary tangles on biopsy
qs.e: The diagnosis of Parkinson's disease is confirmed symptomatically by a positive response to L-DOPA treatment. Neurofibrillary tangles are associated with Alzheimer's, PrPsc detection is for prion diseases, and cortical atrophy is not the primary diagnostic confirmation for Parkinson's.
qs.s: Neurodegenerative Prion Diseases: CJD, Pathology & Rapid Dementia: MCQs

qs.q: During the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease, what is the normal function of the PINK1 and parkin pathway?
o: Phosphorylation of tau to stabilize microtubules
Lysosomal degradation of extracellular prion proteins
qs.e: PINK1 and parkin work together to mediate mitophagy, which is the clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria via proteasomal destruction. Mutations in either gene lead to impaired mitophagy and mitochondrial dysfunction.
qs.s: Neurodegenerative Prion Diseases: CJD, Pathology & Rapid Dementia: MCQs

qs.q: Heterozygous mutations in which lysosomal enzyme represent the most important genetic risk factor for sporadic Parkinson's disease?
qs.e: Mutations in glucocerebrosidase impair the lysosome-autophagy pathway, leading to abnormal alpha-synuclein metabolism. Superoxide dismutase 1 is classically mutated in familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
qs.s: Neurodegenerative Prion Diseases: CJD, Pathology & Rapid Dementia: MCQs

qs.q: Pathogenic mutations in LRRK2 cause Parkinson's disease through which of the following mechanisms?
o: Complete deletion of the tau gene
qs.e: Pathogenic mutations in LRRK2 cause autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease via a gain-of-function mechanism resulting in increased kinase activity. It does not function through free radical detoxification loss, which is characteristic of mutant SOD1.
qs.s: Neurodegenerative Prion Diseases: CJD, Pathology & Rapid Dementia: MCQs

qs.q: Gross examination of the brain in advanced Parkinson's disease typically reveals pallor in which two pigmented structures?
o: Basal nucleus of Meynert and striatum
qs.e: Loss of pigmented catecholaminergic neurons causes characteristic gross pallor of both the substantia nigra and locus ceruleus in Parkinson's disease. The hippocampus and entorhinal cortex are instead targeted earliest in Alzheimer's disease.
qs.s: Neurodegenerative Prion Diseases: CJD, Pathology & Rapid Dementia: MCQs

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Parkinson disease is a neurodegenerative disorder marked by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, causing hypokinetic movement symptoms that improve with levodopa. It is diagnosed clinically, staged with the Hoehn‑Yahr scale, and managed with dopamine replacement and supportive care.

sections.p: Parkinson disease is a progressive movement disorder caused by degeneration of substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons. Diagnosis is clinical, based on the presence of bradykinesia plus at least one of tremor, rigidity or postural instability, and confirmed by a positive response to levodopa.

t.b: Does the patient improve after a trial dose of levodopa? A marked improvement supports Parkinson disease.

sections.p: Severity is staged with the Hoehn‑Yahr scale, ranging from 1 (unilateral symptoms) to 5 (wheelchair or bedridden). Staging guides prognosis and treatment intensity.
Idiopathic Parkinson disease is the most common cause. Genetic mutations (LRRK2, PARK2) and environmental toxins (pesticides, well water) are less frequent but important in low‑resource settings.
Patients present with resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, stooped posture, and festinating gait. Non‑motor features include anosmia, constipation, depression, and sleep disturbances.
Investigations confirm the diagnosis, rule out mimics, and assess complications. In low‑resource settings, clinical assessment is paramount.

t.b: Normal uptake suggests a tremor disorder other than Parkinson disease.
Normal MRI supports idiopathic Parkinson disease.
Abnormal electrolytes may mimic Parkinson disease.

sections.p: Red flags include rapid onset, asymmetric symptoms, severe rigidity, and hallucinations. Complications are falls, aspiration pneumonia, and medication side effects.
b: Severe rigidity or rigidity with dystonia

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause if identified, then start dopamine replacement. Levodopa with carbidopa is first line; dopamine agonists or MAO‑B inhibitors are alternatives. Monitor for dyskinesia and motor fluctuations.
b: MAO‑B inhibitors: modest benefit, avoid with MAO‑A inhibitors

sections.p: Regular follow‑up assesses motor status, medication side effects, and non‑motor symptoms. Early physiotherapy, speech therapy, and nutrition support reduce disability.
Essential tremor, drug‑induced parkinsonism, Wilson disease, and stroke can mimic Parkinson disease.
b: Wilson disease: low ceruloplasmin, Kayser‑Fleischer rings

sections.p: Normal DaT‑scan does not exclude Parkinson disease in early stages; normal MRI may miss small vascular lesions. Low levodopa response can be due to advanced disease.
b: Small vascular lesions may be missed on routine MRI

faq.a: No, it is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder; treatment focuses on symptom control.
Most cases are idiopathic, but some genetic forms exist, especially in families with early onset.
Regular exercise, balanced diet, adequate sleep, and avoidance of neurotoxins reduce symptom progression.
